**Score:** 1.000

name: CI

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:
  # A new advisory lands on an unchanged tree, and the repository can go days without a push. Monday 07:00 UTC;
  # only build-chain answers it (#202).
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 7 * * 1'

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  verify:
    # The weekly run is build-chain's alone.
    if: github.event_name != 'schedule'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@df4cb1c069e1874edd31b4311f1884172cec0e10 # v6
        with:
          persist-credentials: false

      - uses: actions/setup-node@49933ea5288caeca8642d1e84afbd3f7d6820020 # v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          cache: npm

      # Both re:cinq libraries install from the npm registry, whose tarballs ship
      # built code, so no dependency needs a lifecycle script.
      - name: Install
        run: npm ci --ignore-scripts

      # The api tests run against a real mongod, ~100MB that would otherwise be
      # downloaded again on every run. Keyed on the pinned version.
      - name: Cache the mongod the api tests start
        uses: actions/cache@0057852bfaa89a56745cba8c7296529d2fc39830 # v4
        with:
          path: ~/.cache/mongodb-binaries
          key: mongod-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('apps/api/test/mongoTestServer.ts') }}

      # A git or file dependency skips the registry the published libraries exist to prove (#13).
      - name: Keep dependency specifiers on the npm registry
        run: npm run check:dependencies

      # The engine's package root pulls every provider SDK into the browser, and booking data must never touch storage.
      # A test file ships in no bundle, so it may import the engine's recordedFrames; shipped code never does.
      - name: Keep HAL Engine and browser storage out of the web app
        run: |
          if grep -rnE "from ['\"]@re-cinq/hal-engine|import\(['\"]@re-cinq/hal-engine" apps/web/src --exclude='*.test.ts' --exclude='*.test.tsx'; then
            echo "shipped apps/web code must not import @re-cinq/hal-engine" >&2
            exit 1
          fi
          if jq -e '.dependencies["@re-cinq/hal-engine"]' apps/web/package.json > /dev/null; then
            echo "apps/web may list @re-cinq/hal-engine under devDependencies only" >&2
            exit 1
          fi
          if grep -rnE "localStorage|sessionStorage|indexedDB|fetch\(|sendBeacon" apps/web/src/chat apps/web/src/screens apps/web/src/personas; then
            echo "apps/web chat code must not touch browser storage or send anything but the socket" >&2
            exit 1
          fi

      # The model allowlist gates what configuration/ reads; a second reader would bypass it.
      - name: Read model, region and provider settings only in the api configuration
        run: |
          if grep -rnE "process\.env" apps packages --include='*.ts' --include='*.tsx' --exclude-dir=node_modules --exclude-dir=dist \
            | grep -E "MODEL|REGION|LOCATION|PROVIDER" | grep -v '^apps/api/src/configuration/'; then
            echo "only apps/api/src/configuration/ may read a model, region or provider value from process.env" >&2
            exit 1
          fi

      # Declared twice, the band and the model's rule drift apart silently.
      - name: Keep the AI disclosure text in @support-agent/disclosure
        run: |
          if grep -rn "AI-assistent\|kunstig intelligens" apps/api/src apps/web/src; then
            echo "apps must import the AI disclosure from @support-agent/disclosure" >&2
            exit 1
          fi

      # example.com until KU-30 names the domain people who may read a conversation work at.
      - name: Keep human IAM bindings inside infra/terraform/access
        run: node --experimental-strip-types scripts/check-deploy-invariants.ts infra/terraform --domain example.com

      # SC-002: the transport seam only holds if fetchTransport is the one way out; a second caller would skip deadline, retry and redaction.
      - name: Keep network access in the TMS client's transport.ts
        run: |
          if grep -rnE "\bfetch\(|['\"](node:)?(http|https|undici)['\"]" packages/tms-client/src --include='*.ts' | grep -v '^packages/tms-client/src/transport\.ts:'; then
            echo "only packages/tms-client/src/transport.ts may reference fetch, undici, http or https" >&2
            exit 1
          fi

      # The reader prints whole conversations to an operator's terminal: never into a log, onto the network, or into the running service.
      # httpConversationHandler.ts is the deliberate HTTP-adapter exception to the import ban (SC-005/RD-13).
      - name: Keep the conversation reader offline and out of the running service
        run: |
          if grep -rnE "from ['\"](node:)?(http|https|ws|express)['\"]|from ['\"][^'\"]*shared/logger" apps/api/src/reader --exclude="httpConversationHandler.ts"; then
            echo "apps/api/src/reader must not import the application logger, express, http, https or ws (httpConversationHandler.ts is exempt)" >&2
            exit 1
          fi
          if grep -rnE "from ['\"][^'\"]*/reader/" apps/api/src/tools apps/api/src/escalation apps/api/src/start-server.ts; then
            echo "the running service must not reach apps/api/src/reader" >&2
            exit 1
          fi
          if grep -nE "from ['\"](mongodb|[^'\"]*readConversation)" apps/api/src/reader/conversationView.ts; then
            echo "conversationView.ts must stay pure: no mongodb, no readConversation" >&2
            exit 1
          fi
          if grep -nE "from ['\"]mongodb" apps/api/src/reader/httpConversationHandler.ts; then
            echo "httpConversationHandler.ts must not import mongodb" >&2
            exit 1
          fi

      # SC-004: a second timer would be one that shutdown does not clear.
      - name: Keep exactly one setInterval in the api, in shared/periodicJobs.ts
        run: |
          count=$(grep -rn "setInterval(" apps/api/src | wc -l)
          if [ "$count" -ne 1 ]; then
            echo "apps/api/src must hold exactly one setInterval call, found $count; add a job to startPeriodicJobs instead" >&2
            exit 1
          fi

      # Only a reader may reach a vendor; the diff, the CLI and the freshness check run on recorded values.
      - name: Keep vendor SDKs inside the drift readers
        run: |
          if grep -rnE "(from|import\() *['\"](@google-cloud/|@google/genai|@anthropic-ai/|openai|@aws-sdk/|@re-cinq/hal-engine)" \
            packages/control-drift scripts --include='*.ts' --exclude-dir=node_modules --exclude-dir=dist \
            | grep -v '^packages/control-drift/src/readers/'; then
            echo "only packages/control-drift/src/readers/ may import a vendor SDK" >&2
            exit 1
          fi

      - name: Lint
        run: npm run lint

      - name: Typecheck
        run: npm run typecheck

      - name: Test
        run: npm test

      - name: Build
        run: npm run build

      # CR-005: every pull request, whether or not anyone ran the recorder.
      - name: Scan committed TMS fixtures for personal data and credentials
        run: |
          node packages/tms-client/scripts/scan-fixtures.mjs
          node packages/tms-client/scripts/scan-fixtures.mjs apps/api/stand-in-tms

      # Lore's lore_list_tests reads this output; an entry printing anything but {id, name, file} objects breaks it silently.
      - name: Check every Lore test-command list prints a JSON array of tests
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          file=.lore/test-commands.yml
          cwds=$(sed -n 's/^  cwd: //p' "$file")
          lists=$(sed -n 's/^  list: //p' "$file")
          if [ "$(echo "$cwds" | wc -l)" -ne "$(echo "$lists" | wc -l)" ]; then
            echo "$file: every entry needs exactly one cwd and one list" >&2
            exit 1
          fi
          paste -d '\t' <(echo "$cwds") <(echo "$lists") | while IFS=$'\t' read -r cwd list; do
            echo "::group::$cwd: $list"
            (cd "$cwd" && bash -c "$list") > "$RUNNER_TEMP/lore-list.json"
            if ! jq -e 'type == "array" and length > 0 and all(.[]; (.id | type) == "string" and (.name | type) == "string" and (.file | type) == "string")' "$RUNNER_TEMP/lore-list.json" > /dev/null; then
              echo "$cwd: '$list' did not print a non-empty JSON array of {id, name, file}" >&2
              exit 1
            fi
            echo "$(jq length "$RUNNER_TEMP/lore-list.json") tests listed"
            echo "::endgroup::"
          done

      # The chat screen shows persona labels only; a persona's prompt prose or routing keywords in the bundle would publish the agent's instructions.
      - name: Keep persona prompt text out of the web bundle
        run: |
          node --input-type=module -e "
            const {PERSONA_REGISTRY} = await import('./apps/api/dist/prompt/personas.js');
            const prompts = Object.values(PERSONA_REGISTRY.personas).flatMap((persona) => [persona.overlay, ...persona.match]);
            console.log(['PERSONA_VOICE_PLACEHOLDER', ...prompts].filter(Boolean).join('\\n'));
          " > "$RUNNER_TEMP/persona-prompt-text.txt"
          if grep -rnF -f "$RUNNER_TEMP/persona-prompt-text.txt" apps/web/dist; then
            echo "apps/web/dist must not contain a persona overlay, match keyword or PERSONA_VOICE_PLACEHOLDER" >&2
            exit 1
          fi

      # A tool registered without its Danish sentences must fail here, not render a gap.
      - name: Re-record the registered tool names and fail on drift
        run: |
          npm run record-tool-names -w @support-agent/api
          git diff --exit-code apps/web/src/chat/__fixtures__/tool-names.json

  browser:
    # The weekly run is build-chain's alone.
    if: github.event_name != 'schedule'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@df4cb1c069e1874edd31b4311f1884172cec0e10 # v6
        with:
          persist-credentials: false

      - uses: actions/setup-node@49933ea5288caeca8642d1e84afbd3f7d6820020 # v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          cache: npm

      - name: Install
        run: npm ci --ignore-scripts

      - name: Install Chromium
        run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
        working-directory: apps/web

      - name: Browser tests
        run: npm run test:browser

  # A stopped schedule looks like "nothing drifted"; only the age of the newest reading tells them apart.
  # A missing compliance-readings branch fails the second checkout: nothing has ever been read.
  reading-freshness:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@df4cb1c069e1874edd31b4311f1884172cec0e10 # v6
        with:
          persist-credentials: false

      - uses: actions/checkout@df4cb1c069e1874edd31b4311f1884172cec0e10 # v6
        with:
          ref: compliance-readings
          path: compliance-readings
          persist-credentials: false

      - uses: actions/setup-node@49933ea5288caeca8642d1e84afbd3f7d6820020 # v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'

      - name: Check the newest retention reading is under two schedule intervals old
        run: node scripts/check-reading-freshness.ts compliance-readings/observations/retention.jsonl

  chart:
    # The weekly run is build-chain's alone.
    if: github.event_name != 'schedule'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@df4cb1c069e1874edd31b4311f1884172cec0e10 # v6
        with:
          persist-credentials: false

      - uses: azure/setup-helm@9bc31f4ebc9c6b171d7bfbaa5d006ae7abdb4310 # v5.0.1

      # kubeconform publishes no container image, only release tarballs.
      - name: Install kubeconform
        run: |
          curl -fsSL -o kubeconform.tar.gz \
            https://github.com/yannh/kubeconform/releases/download/v0.8.0/kubeconform-linux-amd64.tar.gz
          echo "9bc2bffbf71f261128533edaf912153948b7ff238f9a531ae6d34466ec287883  kubeconform.tar.gz" | sha256sum -c -
          tar -xzf kubeconform.tar.gz kubeconform
          rm kubeconform.tar.gz

      - name: Lint, render and validate the chart
        run: |
          helm lint charts/otto --strict -f deploy/recinq-test.values.yaml \
            --set api.image.tag=ci --set web.image.tag=ci
          helm template otto charts/otto -f deploy/recinq-test.values.yaml \
            --set api.image.tag=ci --set web.image.tag=ci \
            | ./kubeconform -strict -summary \
                -schema-location default \
                -schema-location 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datreeio/CRDs-catalog/main/{{.Group}}/{{.ResourceKind}}_{{.ResourceAPIVersion}}.json'

      # The api refuses to start without a database, so the chart must refuse to
      # render one that would never come up.
      - name: Refuse to render the api without its MongoDB settings
        run: |
          set -o pipefail
          helm template otto charts/otto -f deploy/recinq-test.values.yaml \
            --set api.image.tag=ci --set web.image.tag=ci \
            --show-only templates/api-deployment.yaml \
            | grep -qx '                  key: url'
          for setting in api.mongoSecretName api.mongoDbName; do
            if helm template otto charts/otto -f deploy/recinq-test.values.yaml \
              --set api.image.tag=ci --set web.image.tag=ci --set "$setting=" \
              --show-only templates/api-deployment.yaml; then
              echo "an empty $setting must fail to render" >&2
              exit 1
            fi
          done

      # The retention period is a GDPR decision with no chart default, so the
      # chart must pass it through and refuse to render without one.
      - name: Render CONVERSATION_RETENTION_DAYS and refuse to render without api.conversationRetentionDays
        run: |
          set -o pipefail
          helm template otto charts/otto -f deploy/recinq-test.values.yaml \
            --set api.image.tag=ci --set web.image.tag=ci \
            --show-only templates/api-deployment.yaml \
            | grep -A1 -x '            - name: CONVERSATION_RETENTION_DAYS' \
            | grep -qx '              value: "30"'
          if refusal=$(helm template otto charts/otto -f deploy/recinq-test.values.yaml \
            --set api.image.tag=ci --set web.image.tag=ci --set api.conversationRetentionDays= \
            --show-only templates/api-deployment.yaml 2>&1); then
            echo "an empty api.conversationRetentionDays must fail to render" >&2
            exit 1
          fi; grep -q 'api.conversationRetentionDays is required' <<<"$refusal"

      # Named, the api pod runs as the account Workload Identity binds; unset,
      # the field is absent and the pod falls back to the namespace default.
      - name: Render the api pod with and without api.serviceAccountName
        run: |
          set -o pipefail
          helm template otto charts/otto -f deploy/recinq-test.values.yaml \
            --set api.image.tag=ci --set web.image.tag=ci \
            --show-only templates/api-deployment.yaml \
            | grep -qx '      serviceAccountName: "otto-api"'
          if helm template otto charts/otto -f deploy/recinq-test.values.yaml \
            --set api.image.tag=ci --set web.image.tag=ci --set api.serviceAccountName= \
            --show-only templates/api-deployment.yaml | grep -n "serviceAccountName:"; then
            echo "an empty api.serviceAccountName must render no serviceAccountName field" >&2
            exit 1
          fi

      # Set, every tester is numbered from api.firstCustomerNumber and the login
      # Secret needs no customerNumbers key; unset, the pairs come from that key.
      - name: Render the api's customer numbers with and without api.firstCustomerNumber
        run: |
          set -o pipefail
          helm template otto charts/otto -f deploy/recinq-test.values.yaml \
            --set api.image.tag=ci --set web.image.tag=ci \
            --show-only templates/api-deployment.yaml \
            | grep -A1 -x '            - name: LOGIN_FIRST_CUSTOMER_NUMBER' \
            | grep -qx '              value: "10001"'
          if helm template otto charts/otto -f deploy/recinq-test.values.yaml \
            --set api.image.tag=ci --set web.image.tag=ci \
            --show-only templates/api-deployment.yaml | grep -n "key: customerNumbers"; then
            echo "api.firstCustomerNumber must leave the Secret's customerNumbers key unread" >&2
            exit 1
          fi
          helm template otto charts/otto -f deploy/recinq-test.values.yaml \
            --set api.image.tag=ci --set web.image.tag=ci --set api.firstCustomerNumber= \
            --show-only templates/api-deployment.yaml \
            | grep -qx '                  key: customerNumbers'

      # The api refuses to start without TMS_MODE, and live mode without its key,
      # so the chart refuses to render either; the key only ever comes from a Secret.
      - name: Render the api's TMS mode and refuse an incomplete one
        run: |
          set -o pipefail
          helm template otto charts/otto -f deploy/recinq-test.values.yaml \
            --set api.image.tag=ci --set web.image.tag=ci \
            --show-only templates/api-deployment.yaml \
            | grep -A1 -x '            - name: TMS_MODE' \
            | grep -qx '              value: "stand-in"'
          helm template otto charts/otto -f deploy/recinq-test.values.yaml \
            --set api.image.tag=ci --set web.image.tag=ci --set api.tmsMode=live \
            --set api.tmsBaseUrl=https://tms.example/api/ext/v1 --set api.tmsSecretName=otto-tms \
            --show-only templates/api-deployment.yaml \
            | grep -A4 -x '            - name: TMS_API_KEY' \
            | grep -qx '                  key: apiKey'
          for incomplete in "api.tmsMode=" "api.tmsMode=off" "api.tmsMode=on" "api.tmsMode=live"; do
            if helm template otto charts/otto -f deploy/recinq-test.values.yaml \
              --set api.image.tag=ci --set web.image.tag=ci --set "$incomplete" \
              --show-only templates/api-deployment.yaml >/dev/null 2>&1; then
              echo "$incomplete must fail to render" >&2
              exit 1
            fi
          done

  terraform:
    # The weekly run is build-chain's alone.
    if: github.event_name != 'schedule'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@df4cb1c069e1874edd31b4311f1884172cec0e10 # v6
        with:
          persist-credentials: false

      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@dfe3c3f87815947d99a8997f908cb6525fc44e9e # v4.0.1
        with:
          terraform_version: 1.16.2
          terraform_wrapper: false

      - name: Check formatting
        run: terraform fmt -check -recursive infra/terraform

      - name: Keep the compliance reader free of write and model-invoking roles
        run: |
          if grep -nE 'roles/[A-Za-z.]*(admin|editor|writer|user)"' infra/terraform/recinq-test/compliance-reader.tf; then
            echo "the compliance reader may hold no role ending in admin, editor, writer or user" >&2
            exit 1
          fi

      - name: Validate every root
        run: |
          for root in infra/terraform/modules/otto-deployer infra/terraform/modules/otto-access-identity infra/terraform/modules/otto-runtime-identity infra/terraform/recinq-test infra/terraform/access; do
            terraform -chdir="$root" init -backend=false -input=false
            terraform -chdir="$root" validate
          done

      - name: Validate audit trail routing invariants
        run: ./audit.acceptance.test.sh
        working-directory: infra/terraform/access

  images:
    # No image is built or pushed over an unacknowledged high advisory or an unpinned action (#202).
    needs: [verify, chart, build-chain]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
    strategy:
      matrix:
        component: [api, web]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@df4cb1c069e1874edd31b4311f1884172cec0e10 # v6
        with:
          persist-credentials: false

      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@37fe631027851001ddb9b187196cc803df7f5f0e # v4.3.0

      - uses: docker/login-action@dbcb813823bdd20940b903addbd779551569679f # v4.6.0
        if: github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - id: meta
        uses: docker/metadata-action@dc802804100637a589fabce1cb79ff13a1411302 # v6.2.0
        with:
          images: ghcr.io/re-cinq/otto-${{ matrix.component }}
          tags: |
            type=sha,format=long,prefix=
            type=raw,value=latest,enable={{is_default_branch}}

      # Pull requests build the image to prove the Dockerfile; only main pushes it.
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@53b7df96c91f9c12dcc8a07bcb9ccacbed38856a # v7.3.0
        with:
          context: .
          target: ${{ matrix.component }}
          push: ${{ github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' }}
          tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
          labels: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.labels }}
          cache-from: type=gha,scope=${{ matrix.component }}
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max,scope=${{ matrix.component }}

  deploy:
    needs: images
    if: github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    concurrency:
      group: deploy-recinq-test
      cancel-in-progress: false
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@df4cb1c069e1874edd31b4311f1884172cec0e10 # v6
        with:
          persist-credentials: false

      - uses: google-github-actions/auth@7c6bc770dae815cd3e89ee6cdf493a5fab2cc093 # v3
        with:
          workload_identity_provider: ${{ secrets.GCP_WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_PROVIDER }}
          service_account: ${{ secrets.GCP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT }}

      - uses: google-github-actions/get-gke-credentials@3da1e46a907576cefaa90c484278bb5b259dd395 # v3.0.0
        with:
          cluster_name: ${{ vars.GKE_CLUSTER_NAME }}
          location: europe-west1
          project_id: ${{ vars.GCP_PROJECT_ID }}

      - uses: azure/setup-helm@9bc31f4ebc9c6b171d7bfbaa5d006ae7abdb4310 # v5.0.1

      # Every release sends the full values, never --reuse-values: reused values
      # skip new chart defaults (Lore's nil-pointer outage). No --wait, which
      # wedges on Autopilot; the rollout step below gates instead. The deployer
      # administers only the otto namespace, which infra/terraform/recinq-test creates.
      - name: Release to the re:cinq test environment
        run: |

## **Crafting the Email Autopilot Workflow in n8n**

With the architecture defined, let's dive into the n8n canvas. This workflow orchestrates a series of checks and AI-driven actions to build context before ever drafting a reply. Before you begin, ensure you have credentials configured in n8n for Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Drive, Slack, and any CRM API you wish to connect.

![Conceptual n8n workflow for Email Autopilot](/blog-img/ai-email-autopilot.webp)

### **Part 1: The Gatekeeper – Triage and Filtering**

The workflow starts by protecting you from noise.

1.  **Gmail Trigger & Remove Duplicates:** The workflow kicks off with a `Gmail Trigger` that polls for new messages. It uses a filter to ignore mail from common no-reply addresses and mail sent from yourself. It immediately passes the email to a `Remove Duplicates` node to prevent re-processing.

2.  **Assess if Email Requires an Answer (`AI Agent`):** The first AI step is a simple triage. The email content is passed to a lightweight `AI Agent` powered by a fast model like `gemini-1.5-flash-latest`. Its only job is to decide if the email is substantive or junk.

    **The Triage Prompt:**
    ```
    Your task is to assess if the message requires a response. Return in JSON format true if it does, false otherwise. Also pass on the id, threadId, content, sender name, email and subject.

    Marketing emails don't require a response.
  
    Example:
    {
      "requiresResponse": true,
      "id": "12345",
      "threadId": "67890",
      "content": "...",
      "name": "Jim Smith",
      "email": "jim@example.com",
      "subject": "Catching up"
    }
    ```

3.  **JSON Parser & If Node:** A `Code` node parses the AI's JSON output, and an `If` node checks if `requiresResponse` is `true`. If not, the workflow stops. If it is, the email is passed to the main agent.

### **Part 2: The Brain – The Context-Aware AI Agent**

This is the heart of the workflow. We use a sophisticated `AI Agent` node with a detailed system prompt that defines its identity, mission, and rules of engagement.

**The Main Agent's System Prompt:**

👤 Identity
You are an advanced AI assistant integrated into an email client, acting on behalf of a user named Michael. Your persona is that of an efficient, proactive, and exceptionally thorough executive assistant.

🎯 Core Mission & Thinking Process
Your central mission is to generate a draft email reply that is so accurate and well-informed that Michael can send it with minimal to no edits. To achieve this, you must follow a strict, multi-step process for every email you handle.

Step 1: Immediate Triage
Quickly scan the incoming email to identify the sender, their primary request, and the language of the message (English or German).

Step 2: Autonomous Context Gathering (Mandatory)
Before you begin writing, you must autonomously gather a complete picture of the situation using your available tools.

Check the Calendar (Calendar tool): To understand Michael's current and future availability.

Review Past Conversations (Email tool): To understand the relationship and communication style with the sender.

Find Related Documents (Google Drive tool): To find project notes, agendas, or any shared documents.

Verify Contact Details (CRM/Apollo): To understand the sender's role and importance.

Step 3: Synthesize and Strategize
Once your tool use is complete, pause and create a silent, internal summary of all the information you've gathered.

Step 4: Draft the Response

Language Matching: Critically, you must respond in the same language as the incoming email. If the sender writes in German, your draft must be entirely in German.

Directly address the sender's request.

Seamlessly weave in the context you found.

Mirror the established tone from past emails.

Conclude with "Best regards, Michael" (or the German equivalent).

🛠️ Rules for Tool Use

Never Assume, Always Verify. Use a tool if the information can be found.

Do not refer to the names of your tools in the final draft. Instead of "The Calendar tool shows you are busy," say, "It looks like my schedule is packed today."

### **Part 3: The Senses – Assembling the Toolkit**

The real power of this agent comes from the tools we give it. The `AI Agent` node has several tool nodes connected to it:
* **Google Calendar Tool:** Configured to `getAll` events, allowing the agent to check for free/busy slots.
* **Gmail Tool:** Configured to `getAll` messages, which the agent can use to search for past conversations with the sender.
* **Google Drive Tool:** Configured to `search` for files and folders, enabling the agent to find relevant documents by searching for the sender's name or company.
* **HTTP Request Tool:** Configured to query a CRM like Apollo.io. The agent can use this to fetch the sender's job title and company information, adding crucial business context.

The AI agent will intelligently decide which of these tools to use, in what order, based on the content of the email.

### **Part 4: The Safety Net – Human-in-the-Loop Approval**

We believe in empowerment, not full, unchecked autonomy. The output of the AI Agent is a carefully drafted message, but it isn't sent automatically.

1.  **Send message and wait for response (`Slack` Node):** The generated draft is sent to a private Slack channel or DM. This node is configured to post the message along with two action buttons: "Approve" and "Deny." The workflow then pauses, waiting for your input.

2.  **If Node:** This node checks the response from Slack. If you click "Approve," the workflow continues to the final step. If you click "Deny," it stops.

3.  **Gmail - Create Draft (`Gmail` Node):** Upon approval, the final node takes the AI-generated text and creates a new **draft** in your Gmail, correctly threaded to the original conversation. It's ready for a final glance and for you to personally hit "Send."

### **Putting It All Together: A Sample Interaction**

Let's see the magic in action with the scenario from earlier.

1.  **Email In:** You receive an email from `jim@partner-org.com`: "Hey Michael, great chat last week. Got time to connect tomorrow to discuss the partnership details?"

## What Makes a System AI Native?

AI Native isn't about adding AI features to existing applications - it's about fundamentally rethinking how systems are designed, built, and operated. An AI Native system has intelligence built into its core architecture, enabling continuous learning, autonomous decision-making, and adaptive behavior.

Key characteristics of AI Native systems include:

- **Intelligent by Default:** AI capabilities are embedded throughout the system, not bolted on as afterthoughts
- **Continuous Learning:** Systems automatically improve based on user interactions and data patterns
- **Autonomous Operations:** Self-healing, self-scaling, and self-optimizing infrastructure
- **Context-Aware:** Understanding user intent, environmental conditions, and business context
- **Adaptive Interfaces:** User experiences that evolve based on individual preferences and behaviors

Think of how modern recommendation systems work - they don't just serve static content but continuously learn from user behavior to improve recommendations. AI Native extends this concept across entire technology stacks.

### How to Build AI Native Systems: Beyond Traditional Software Development

Traditional software development follows predictable patterns: requirements gathering, design, implementation, testing, deployment. AI Native development is fundamentally different. It's iterative, experimental, and driven by data rather than rigid specifications.

**Key differences in AI Native development:**

- **Data is the new code** - The quality and quantity of training data often matters more than algorithmic sophistication
- **Models evolve continuously** - Unlike traditional software versions, AI models improve through ongoing training and fine-tuning
- **Experimentation is core** - A/B testing, model comparisons, and hypothesis-driven development become standard practices
- **Observability is critical** - Monitoring model performance, data drift, and prediction accuracy requires new tooling and approaches

This shift requires new skills, tools, and organizational structures. Engineering teams need to understand machine learning pipelines, data scientists need to think about production systems, and operations teams need to manage model lifecycles.

### What Infrastructure Do You Need for AI Native Systems?

Just as Cloud Native required new infrastructure patterns (containers, orchestration, service mesh, ...), AI Native demands its own architectural pattern built upon Cloud Native foundations. One of the most popular key pattern that enables AI Native systems is **FTI Architecture**, a unified architectural approach that separates machine learning workloads into three distinct, independently managed pipelines: Feature Pipeline, Training Pipeline, and Inference Pipeline.

### How Does FTI Architecture Build on Cloud Native Microservices?

FTI Architecture is the microservices pattern for AI systems. It applies Cloud Native principles specifically to machine learning workloads, providing the same benefits of separation of concerns, independent scaling, and fault isolation that made Cloud Native successful. This architectural pattern streamlines the development, deployment, and maintenance of machine learning models across their entire lifecycle.

**Feature Pipeline:**
This stage deals with collecting, processing, and transforming raw data into usable features for AI models.

- **Data Ingestion:** Raw data is collected in real-time and from recorded sources, including sensor data, user interactions, and external system communications
- **Data Preprocessing & Fusion:** Data is cleaned, synchronized, and fused from multiple sources to create comprehensive datasets. Noise reduction and calibration are critical for data quality
- **Feature Engineering:** Relevant features are extracted and transformed. This includes identifying patterns, calculating derived metrics, and creating feature representations optimized for model consumption
- **Feature Store:** Processed features are stored, versioned, and managed in centralized repositories. This enables consistent feature access for both training and inference while supporting data drift detection
- **Cloud Native Alignment:** Operates like data API gateways, providing standardized interfaces and microservices-based data processing
- **Technology Stack:** [Pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org/), [Polars](https://www.pola.rs/), [Apache Spark](https://spark.apache.org/), [DBT](https://www.getdbt.com/), [Apache Flink](https://flink.apache.org/), [Bytewax](https://github.com/bytewax/bytewax), [Feast](https://feast.dev/), [Tecton](https://www.tecton.ai/), or custom containerized microservices

**Training Pipeline:**
This is where AI models learn to perform their tasks, typically run offline in powerful compute environments.

- **Model Selection:** Appropriate model architectures are chosen based on the problem domain (e.g., deep neural networks for perception, reinforcement learning for decision-making)
- **Model Training & Validation:** Models are trained using curated features and corresponding labels. Rigorous validation against diverse datasets ensures accuracy and generalization through simulation and controlled testing
- **Model Registry:** Trained and validated models are versioned and stored with performance metrics and training metadata. This enables rollback capabilities and comprehensive auditability
- **Continuous Learning:** The pipeline supports retraining models as new data becomes available or new scenarios are encountered, ensuring continuous system improvement
- **Cloud Native Alignment:** Functions as batch processing services with resource-intensive, scheduled workloads that can scale elastically
- **Technology Stack:** [PyTorch](https://pytorch.org/), [TensorFlow](https://www.tensorflow.org/), [Scikit-Learn](https://scikit-learn.org/), [XGBoost](https://xgboost.ai/), [JAX](https://docs.jax.dev/), [Hugging Face Transformers](https://huggingface.co/transformers/), [Kubeflow](https://www.kubeflow.org/), [MLflow](https://mlflow.org/), [ZenML](https://zenml.io/), [Apache Airflow](https://airflow.apache.org/), or custom training orchestrators

**Inference Pipeline:**
This is the real-time execution of trained models in production environments to generate predictions and drive actions.

- **Real-time Feature Ingestion:** Live data feeds into feature extraction modules, optimized for low-latency processing
- **Model Deployment & Execution:** Approved models from the model registry are deployed onto production compute units (CPUs, GPUs, specialized AI accelerators)
- **Prediction & Decision Making:** Models analyze input data to generate predictions, classify scenarios, and recommend actions based on learned patterns
- **Actuation:** Predictions are translated into actionable outputs that drive downstream systems and user experiences
- **Monitoring & Logging:** Pipeline performance and model predictions are continuously monitored and logged for analysis, error detection, and future retraining feedback
- **Cloud Native Alignment:** Operates like traditional API services but optimized for AI-specific requirements including model versioning and A/B testing
- **Technology Stack:** [PyTorch](https://pytorch.org/), [TensorFlow](https://www.tensorflow.org/), [Scikit-Learn](https://scikit-learn.org/), [XGBoost](https://xgboost.ai/), [JAX](https://docs.jax.dev/), [TensorFlow Serving](https://www.tensorflow.org/tfx/guide/serving), [MLflow Model Serving](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/models.html#deploy-mlflow-models), [KServe](https://kserve.github.io/website/), [NVIDIA Triton](https://developer.nvidia.com/nvidia-triton-inference-server), or custom inference APIs

**Model Management Layer:**

- Experiment tracking for comparing model performance across the FTI pipeline using [Comet ML](https://www.comet.com/), [MLflow](https://mlflow.org/), or [Weights & Biases](https://wandb.ai/)
- Model registries that coordinate deployment from Training Pipeline to Inference Pipeline, including [Hugging Face Model Hub](https://huggingface.co/models) for pre-trained models
- Managed services like [Google Vertex AI Model Registry](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/model-registry/introduction), [AWS SageMaker Model Registry](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/model-registry.html), or [Azure Machine Learning model management](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/machine-learning/concept-model-management-and-deployment)
- **FTI Integration:** Orchestrates the flow of model artifacts between pipelines with proper versioning and governance

- Real-time data streaming using [Apache Kafka](https://kafka.apache.org/) or similar platforms to feed Feature Pipeline
- Feature stores like [Feast](https://feast.dev/) or [Tecton](https://www.tecton.ai/) for consistent feature access across all pipelines
- Vector databases like [Qdrant](https://qdrant.tech/), [Pinecone](https://www.pinecone.io/), or [Weaviate](https://weaviate.io/) for storing embeddings and similarity search

- Managed services like [Google Cloud Dataflow](https://cloud.google.com/dataflow), [AWS Kinesis Data Streams](https://aws.amazon.com/kinesis/data-streams/), or [Azure Event Hubs](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/services/event-hubs/) for data processing
- **FTI Integration:** Ensures data consistency and lineage from Feature Pipeline through Training Pipeline to Inference Pipeline

- Edge computing nodes for low-latency Inference Pipeline applications
- Auto-scaling systems handling variable computational demands across all three pipelines
- Managed compute services like [Google Cloud AI Platform](https://cloud.google.com/ai-platform), [AWS SageMaker](https://aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/), or [Azure Machine Learning](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/services/machine-learning/) for scalable ML workloads

AI Native is the next disruptive wave, fundamentally changing how we build software. Our experience shows organizations pushing "AI" for cost-cutting, like an off-the-shelf chatbot, without a corresponding shift in workflow or upskilling. AI Native is about building with AI at its core, enabling learning, adaptation, and automating operations. GenAI is driving excitement, but the future of AI Native is still forming.

The **pioneering imperative** is crucial: don't wait. Small, autonomous teams should explore AI, run experiments, and upskill the workforce now. ### Why FTI Architecture Accelerates AI Native Transformation

Organizations that successfully adopt FTI Architecture gain significant advantages in their AI Native transformation:

**Independent Pipeline Scaling:** Just as Cloud Native microservices enabled independent team ownership, FTI Architecture allows specialized teams to own Feature Pipeline, Training Pipeline, and Inference Pipeline operations separately. This reduces coordination overhead and enables faster iteration cycles.

**Technology Flexibility per Pipeline:** Each pipeline can use technologies optimized for its specific workload patterns. Feature Pipeline might leverage Apache Spark for large-scale data processing, Training Pipeline might use PyTorch with CUDA for model development, and Inference Pipeline might use TensorFlow for optimized edge deployment.

**Fault Isolation Across Pipelines:** Problems in one pipeline don't cascade to others. A Training Pipeline failure doesn't impact real-time Inference Pipeline operations, and Feature Pipeline changes can be tested independently before affecting model performance.

**Resource Optimization by Workload:** Organizations can right-size infrastructure for each pipeline type. GPU clusters scale up during Training Pipeline cycles, Feature Pipeline maintains steady-state processing capacity, and Inference Pipeline auto-scales with user demand patterns.

**Governance and Compliance Boundaries:** FTI separation enables granular security controls and audit trails. name: CI

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  # Manual runs: re-checking a branch against a moved main, or confirming a gate after
  # changing one, without pushing an empty commit.
  workflow_dispatch:
  # An advisory published after a merge is invisible until someone opens a pull request, and this
  # repository can go days without one. Monday 07:00 UTC; only `build-chain` answers it.
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 7 * * 1'

# Every job here only reads the checkout; the repo default is write.
permissions:
  contents: read

# A newer push to the same branch supersedes an in-flight run. main is exempt:
# every commit there should have its own recorded result.
concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.ref != 'refs/heads/main' }}

jobs:
  verify:
    name: Verify
    # The scheduled run exists for the dependency audit; re-running the suite on an unchanged
    # tree every Monday would report nothing new.
    if: github.event_name != 'schedule'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
          # Full history, not for this job but for the spec anchor check below:
          # it resolves cited content from
          # origin/main, which a shallow clone cannot serve.
          fetch-depth: 0

      - uses: actions/setup-node@949feb2413d6458794dcd2491c4babbbce0c15c1 # v7.1.0
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          cache: npm

      # --ignore-scripts so `prepare` does not build on install: what a lifecycle script
      # runs is out of this workflow's control, and the Build step below is where a broken
      # compile should be reported. Type check catches it earlier still.
      - name: Install
        run: npm ci --ignore-scripts

      # Every `npm run` step below is one link of the `verify` script in
      # package.json, in the same order - scripts/verify-script.test.ts holds
      # the two together - and kept as separate steps so a red run names the
      # gate that failed rather than a single opaque command.
      - name: Type check
        run: npm run typecheck

      # example/ is outside tsconfig.json's rootDir, so nothing checked the one
      # file the README and the guide are written against.
      - name: Type check the example
        run: npm run typecheck:example

      - name: Lint (--max-warnings 0)
        run: npm run eslint

      # Reports, never blocks. The one rule it runs is `warn`, so the step exits
      # 0 on its own and carries no continue-on-error: a non-zero exit here now
      # means the config itself broke, and that should fail. Its findings render
      # as warning annotations rather than failures, which is what a report on a
      # passing check should look like.
      #
      # require-statement-links counts spec statements with no test behind them.
      # Most of what it reports needs a test written rather than a line changed,
      # so the count is meant to be visible on every run and to fall over time.
      # Its test-side mirror, require-spec-link, is satisfied and gates in the
      # Lint step above. Never add a rule here to escape a red gate -
      # eslint.config.backlog.mjs says what belongs.
      - name: Spec traceability backlog (report)
        run: npm run lint:backlog

      - name: Format check
        run: npm run prettier:check

      # Runs the whole suite and fails it on the committed coverage floor in
      # jest.config.js, so this is the test gate rather than an extra pass.
      - name: Test (with coverage floor)
        run: npm run test:coverage

      - name: Build
        run: npm run build

      # Anchors drift silently: a cited file gaining or losing lines above the
      # cited one leaves the link pointing at different content, and the spec
      # still reads as cited. Resolves content at origin/main, which the
      # fetch-depth: 0 above exists to provide. A red check is fixed by running
      # `node scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.mjs` and committing the result.
      - name: Spec anchor check
        run: node scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.mjs --check origin/main

      # A citation counts as coverage only in its statement's trailing
      # parenthetical; one written mid-statement is dropped by the Lore job in silence,
      # so the spec reads as cited while its coverage is zero. A red check is
      # fixed by moving the link to the end of its statement, never by deleting
      # it (AGENTS.md § Spec Test Links).

      - name: Documented code blocks
        run: npm run docs:check

      - name: Documented paths resolve
        run: npm run docs:check-paths

      - name: Spec citations name their test

      - name: Spec status

      - name: Audit (high and above)

        with:
          persist-credentials: false

      - uses: actions/setup-node@949feb2413d6458794dcd2491c4babbbce0c15c1 # v7.1.0
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          cache: npm

      - name: Install (no build)
        run: npm ci --ignore-scripts

      - name: Swap in driver 6
        run: npm install --no-save --ignore-scripts mongodb@6

      - name: Type check
        run: npm run typecheck

      # --ignore-scripts skipped mongodb-memory-server's postinstall, so the first suite to start would download mongod,
      # and two suites starting together raced for one file. Fetched once here, before any worker starts.
      - name: Fetch the mongod binary once
        run: node node_modules/mongodb-memory-server/postinstall.js

      - name: Test the Mongo store
        run: npm test -- src/infrastructure/stores/mongo

  # consumer receives it - packed, installed outside this tree, with no optional
  # peer present. Everything else here tests the source in place, where every
  # dependency is already installed and every one of these failures is invisible.

    name: Smoke (packed tarball)
    if: github.event_name != 'schedule'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false

      - uses: actions/setup-node@949feb2413d6458794dcd2491c4babbbce0c15c1 # v7.1.0
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          cache: npm

      - name: Install (no build)
        run: npm ci --ignore-scripts

      # Explicit, rather than relying on `npm pack` to trigger `prepare`: a build failure should be

}

log_warning() {
    echo "WARNING: $1" >&2
}

# Cleanup function for temporary files
cleanup() {

    exit $exit_code
}

# Set up cleanup trap
trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM

#==============================================================================
# Validation Functions

validate_environment() {
    # Check if we have a current branch/feature (git or non-git)
    if [[ -z "$CURRENT_BRANCH" ]]; then
        log_error "Unable to determine current feature"
        if [[ "$HAS_GIT" == "true" ]]; then
            log_info "Make sure you're on a feature branch"

        fi
        exit 1
    fi
    
    # Check if plan.md exists
    if [[ ! -f "$NEW_PLAN" ]]; then
        log_error "No plan.md found at $NEW_PLAN"
        log_info "Make sure you're working on a feature with a corresponding spec directory"
        if [[ "$HAS_GIT" != "true" ]]; then
            log_info "Use: export SPECIFY_FEATURE=your-feature-name or create a new feature first"
        fi
        exit 1
    fi

#==============================================================================
# Plan Parsing Functions

extract_plan_field() {
    local field_pattern="$1"
    local plan_file="$2"
    
    grep "^\*\*${field_pattern}\*\*: " "$plan_file" 2>/dev/null | \
        head -1 | \
        sed "s|^\*\*${field_pattern}\*\*: ||" | \
        sed 's/^[ \t]*//;s/[ \t]*$//' | \
        grep -v "NEEDS CLARIFICATION" | \
        grep -v "^N/A$" || echo ""
}

parse_plan_data() {
    local plan_file="$1"
    
    if [[ ! -f "$plan_file" ]]; then
        log_error "Plan file not found: $plan_file"
        return 1
    fi
    
    if [[ ! -r "$plan_file" ]]; then
        log_error "Plan file is not readable: $plan_file"
        return 1
    fi
    
    log_info "Parsing plan data from $plan_file"
    
    NEW_LANG=$(extract_plan_field "Language/Version" "$plan_file")
    NEW_FRAMEWORK=$(extract_plan_field "Primary Dependencies" "$plan_file")
    NEW_DB=$(extract_plan_field "Storage" "$plan_file")
    NEW_PROJECT_TYPE=$(extract_plan_field "Project Type" "$plan_file")
    
    # Log what we found
    if [[ -n "$NEW_LANG" ]]; then
        log_info "Found language: $NEW_LANG"

    fi

    if [[ ${#parts[@]} -eq 0 ]]; then
        echo ""
    elif [[ ${#parts[@]} -eq 1 ]]; then
        echo "${parts[0]}"
    else
        # Join multiple parts with " + "
        local result="${parts[0]}"
        for ((i=1; i<${#parts[@]}; i++)); do

    local temp_file="$2"

    local current_date="$4"

    # Perform substitutions with error checking using safer approach

    local escaped_framework=$(printf '%s\n' "$NEW_FRAMEWORK" | sed 's/[\[\.*^$()+{}|]/\\&/g')

    elif [[ -n "$escaped_lang" ]]; then
        tech_stack="- $escaped_lang ($escaped_branch)"
    elif [[ -n "$escaped_framework" ]]; then
        tech_stack="- $escaped_framework ($escaped_branch)"
    else
        tech_stack="- ($escaped_branch)"
    fi

        recent_change="- $escaped_branch: Added $escaped_lang + $escaped_framework"
    elif [[ -n "$escaped_lang" ]]; then
        recent_change="- $escaped_branch: Added $escaped_lang"
    elif [[ -n "$escaped_framework" ]]; then
        recent_change="- $escaped_branch: Added $escaped_framework"
    else
        recent_change="- $escaped_branch: Added"
    fi

        "s|\[DATE\]|$current_date|"

        "s|\[ACTUAL STRUCTURE FROM PLANS\]|$project_structure|g"

            return 1
        fi
    done

    # Clean up backup files
    rm -f "$temp_file.bak" "$temp_file.bak2"
    
    return 0
}
